Price Travel Curves

Research method: how the score is made, and how far to trust it

This page counts, over ten years of gold futures (GC), when gold moves during your hours, 12:00 to 01:00 Singapore time, with the New York time beside it. Each half hour of each trade date is labelled a trend, a swing or a whipsaw from your 5-minute chart (the 15-minute and the 1-minute chart are a button away), and the points card adds those labels up into a score per 100 days.

Curve lab

Curve lab. These tabs are the original experiment and are kept apart from the gold study. They ask one question of a set of price bars: after price has moved, how much of that move is still there some minutes later? To judge it, the lab compares the real bars with a "coin flip" version of them: the same bars, but with the direction of every move decided by the toss of a coin, so it has no trends and no reversals by construction. A real line above the coin-flip line means moves tended to carry on; below it, moves tended to be taken back; inside the shaded band, the bars cannot be told apart from the coin. Nothing on the two gold tabs uses this comparison.

Of the ground price covers over h bars, high to low, how much is still kept at the end? That share is the kept-move curve K(h). A trend keeps more as h grows, pullbacks included. A range keeps less, wherever its highs and lows land. Whipsaw and overlapping candles keep little from the first bar. The travel curve V(h) below shows the squared move behind it. Moves are in basis points (1 bp = 0.01% of price).

Set the curve

The thick grey line is the truth you set with the knobs. The dots are what the method measures on candles simulated from the same knobs. When days are few or bars are short, the method can't recover every part, and it must say so.

The grey ribbon is where a coin flip with exactly these candles lands: each bar is mirrored up or down at random, which keeps its size and wicks and removes direction. Above the ribbon and rising: trend, pullbacks included. Below it, or rising then falling back: range. Low from the first bar: whipsaw or overlapping candles.     What makes up the move at Href

    Shares of the squared move at Href, from the travel-curve fit, with 5–95% ranges once the fit check finishes. They describe the curve; the verdict comes from the kept-move curve above. A trend over H bars can also be one leg of a longer swing.

    What this study can and cannot tell you

    The study counts what gold did in each half hour of your day over ten years: how far it travelled, and whether its 1-minute chart read as a trend, a swing or a whipsaw. Every figure is a count or a size, with the number of days behind it. A figure from fewer than 30 days is greyed and marked "too few days".

    To check that a pattern is not a one-off, the ten years are split in two, 2015–2021 and 2022–2026. A half hour is called busy or idle only when both periods agree, and the cards say whether a figure is the same in both periods or not the same in both periods.

    The page cannot tell you which way a move will go, and when to pay attention is not when to trade. No trade was tested here: use the figures to choose when to watch, and test your own entries, exits and costs separately.

    Three limits:

    • After the fact: a half hour's label uses the whole half hour, so it describes it afterwards. It is not a signal you could have taken at its start.
    • News days: a few big news days (jobs report, CPI, FOMC) can shape a half hour's figures; the cards name them where they matter.
    • The recent days: they are one stretch of time set beside ten years; they show where the ten-year schedule held, not a new schedule.
    Where the gold numbers come from

    Every figure on the two gold tabs comes from the built-in 1-minute bars of gold futures, 2015-11 to 2026-04 for the ten years and the trade dates after them for the recent days, cleaned as the import summary on each tab describes. The ten-year figures were computed once, when the page was built, from the same code.

    Words used on the two gold tabs, explained in the glossary: typical move, typical half hour, variance ratio, slot-day, trend, swing and whipsaw, 20MA and Bollinger Bands (20, 2), both periods, too few days, Singapore and New York time.

    Glossary
    Typical move
    How far gold usually moves in five minutes at a time of day, in dollars an ounce at the middle closing price of the last 252 trade dates. About two moves in three are smaller.
    Typical half hour
    The middle half hour of the whole trading day, the yardstick the watch panel measures every half hour against: 1.0× means as busy as that, 2× means gold travels twice as far.
    Variance ratio
    The watch panel's measure of how busy a half hour is: its average squared five-minute move divided by that of the typical half hour (1.0 = typical). The bars show its square root, the distance gold travels.
    Slot-day
    One half hour (or quarter hour) on one trade date, counted only when the whole slot has bars.
    Trend, swing and whipsaw
    The three labels the points card gives each slot-day, read from the 1-minute chart with the 20MA, the Bollinger Bands (20, 2) and the 5-minute average; the points card explains each rule and lets you set the weights.
    20MA and Bollinger Bands (20, 2)
    The average of the last 20 one-minute closes, and two lines above and below it, each twice the usual spread of those 20 closes away from the average.
    Both periods
    2015 to 2021 and 2022 to 2026, each counted on its own. "The same in both periods" means the two agree; "not the same in both periods" means they do not.
    Too few days
    A figure counted on fewer than 30 days. It is shown greyed: it can show an exception, not a pattern.
    Singapore and New York time
    Times are in Singapore time (SGT) with New York time beside them. New York is 13 hours behind Singapore in US winter and 12 hours behind in US summer.

    What these curves can and cannot tell you

    "Trend" or "Range" on a slot means its moves kept going, or came back, more than in coin-flip copies of its own candles: worth an out-of-sample test with your own entries, exits and costs, not permission to trade. "No directional pattern" means the slot keeps its moves like a coin flip, or leans a little to range or trend by less than the effect floor: the slot table finds no direction there. It says nothing about how much gold moves at that time; the watch schedule at the top and the time-of-day card do. No trading costs were measured on this page. "Slot too short" means fewer than 8 bars of horizon fit in the slot. "Data problem" means the data check found mixed contracts, interleaved series, bars outside the session or an uneven bar interval, and no slot is labelled until the file is fixed.

    The page cannot tell you which way a move will go, and when to pay attention is not when to trade.

    Where the GC numbers come from

    The answers at the top of the CSV 10y tab are computed from the built-in data, as are the slot table and the cards below it. The offline studies behind the method are in dev/v4_robust, dev/v4_mixture and dev/v4_timing.

    The average kept move against coin-flip copies (the line under the slot table) is a descriptive size: about 0.6 to 1.1 tick per H-bar pair in 2015 to 2021 and 0.8 to 1.7 ticks in 2022 to 2026 (offline study). In 2017 to 2019, when a 1-minute bar spanned about 2.7 ticks, bid-ask bounce alone produces a difference of this size in a simulated random walk. The lean itself is about twice what bounce gives and is not explained by it. Treat it as texture, not as an edge.

    The coin-flip range comes from your own candles, so wicks, spread and volatility changes are already in it. It assumes one bar's direction says nothing about the next. On a pure random walk, about 2 to 4 slots in 100 still get Trend or Range by chance, more often on short slots. Scan 24 slots and expect about 1 false label, so look for slots that keep their label when you change the slot length or the date range.

    The two whipsaw limits, candle overlap 0.55 and R(3) 0.75 (under "Details: the rule checks and limits"), are judgement calls. Moving them relabels the selected slot's verdict and rows computed in your browser; the precomputed rows of the 10-year table keep the labels they were built with. Bar size matters: a dead market on 1-minute bars may look fine on 5-minute bars.

    Both curves describe how price moved in a slot after the fact, and a few event days can shape them. They also use closes that were not known at the slot's start. Use them to pick slots and ideas to test. The real test is a simple after-cost strategy probe (trend-follow and band-fade) in the research protocol.

    Three ways a slot result can mislead you:

    • Look-ahead: the curve for a slot uses the whole slot, so it describes the slot after the fact. It is not a signal you could have taken at the slot's open.
    • Carry-over: when moves may run past the slot end, a quiet slot can inherit the next slot's behaviour. Compare the result with the box on and off.
    • Boundary: short slots cut off the long horizons, so H drops. A swing longer than the slot looks like a trend inside it, and short slots with few days often read Unclear. Read H before trusting a verdict.

    Words used on this page, explained in the glossary: typical move, big leg, sign-flipped copies, coin-flip copies, kept move, lean, median and 1% / 99% lines, z, R(3), candle overlap, variance ratio, slot-day, trend day, whipsaw-type day, Whipsaw slot verdict, Wilson interval, rank correlation, family-wise chance, both halves of the data.

    Glossary
    Typical move
    One standard deviation of the 5-minute move at a time of day, in dollars at the median close of the last 252 trade dates. About two moves in three are smaller.
    Big leg
    A move of at least 1.5 times the typical one-hour move of the previous 20 days. It "shows itself" when it has travelled that far; "usually over by" is the median time from then to its end.
    Sign-flipped copies
    The same day with every 5-minute step mirrored up or down at random: the sizes and their times stay, the direction goes. Anything the copies show just as often is the volatility clock, not direction.
    Coin-flip copies
    The slot's own candles with each bar mirrored up or down at random, which keeps its size and wicks and removes direction. The slot table compares every slot with 300 of them.
    Kept move K(h)
    Of the ground price covers over h bars, high to low, the share still kept at the end. A coin flip keeps about half.
    Lean
    K at the slot's last horizon minus the coin-flip copies' median. Below 0: the slot keeps less of its moves than a coin flip (reversal); above 0: more (continuation).
    Median and 1% / 99% lines
    The middle and the outer edges of the coin-flip copies' K. A label needs K beyond the 1% or 99% line and a lean larger than the effect floor.
    z
    The lean divided by the spread of the coin-flip copies. A large z with a tiny lean means a very sure tiny lean, not a strong effect.
    R(3)
    The squared 3-bar move divided by the sum of the squared 1-bar moves along the same path. Below 1: pushes get undone; above 1: they continue.
    Candle overlap
    How much consecutive candles sit on top of each other, 0 to 1. High overlap with a low R(3) reads Whipsaw / dead.
    Variance ratio
    The timing card's R(3)-like ratio over 30-minute blocks: below its sign-flip band, moves in that half hour get undone; above it, they are kept.
    Slot-day
    One time-of-day slot on one trade date, counted only when the whole slot has bars.
    Trend day
    A slot-day whose move fewer than 5 in 100 of its mirrored copies match. A coin gives 5 in 100 by construction.
    Whipsaw-type day
    A slot-day the trend-days card labels as pushes undone (W). Not the same thing as the Whipsaw slot verdict.
    Whipsaw slot verdict
    The slot table's label when candle overlap stays high or R(3) stays low across all the slot's days.
    Wilson interval
    A 95% range for a share computed from a count, used for the per-100 rates.
    Rank correlation
    How well two orderings agree, from −1 to 1; 1 means the busy and quiet hours come in the same order.
    Family-wise chance
    The chance that at least one of many slots crosses a line by luck alone, when none really differs.
    Both halves of the data
    2015 to 2021 (discovery) and 2022 to 2026 (holdout), each checked on its own; other files are split at the median date.

    Research method · Gold

    How the score is made

    Ten years of gold futures, in rows of your scoring timeframe. Each row of each day is labelled from the 5MA, 20MA and Bollinger Bands: Trend +3, Swing +1 or Whipsaw −1. A row's score is its average points per 100 days. The page opens on 15-minute rows scored on 1-minute bars.

    Use it to rank the hours of your day. The answer "when to watch" is made from the settings in force.

    Keep in mind

    • Hindsight: a label describes a finished row and says almost nothing about the next.
    • Mostly a volatility clock: the top rows are when gold moves most.
    • The rules and settings were chosen with these ten years in view; only new days can test them.
    • No direction and no entry.
    How a row gets its label

    The data. 3.33 million 1-minute bars of gold futures (GC) from 30 November 2015 to 24 April 2026: 2,420 trade dates, one contract per trade date at its own unadjusted prices (52 contracts). Rows run on the New York clock from 18:00; Singapore is 13 hours ahead in the US winter and 12 in the US summer.

    The row and its chart. Your scoring timeframe sets the row: 15, 30 or 60 minutes. A row is read on the candles of one chart: 15-minute rows on 1-minute bars; 30-minute rows on 5-minute candles or 1-minute bars; 60-minute rows on 5- or 15-minute candles. The 20MA, the bands at ±2 standard deviations and the 5MA are those of that chart, drawn over its candles in order as a continuous chart draws them: on 1-minute bars the 20MA spans 20 minutes, on 5-minute candles 100 minutes. Every "which side" and "did it touch" decision is made on whole cents.

    Which rows count. A row on a day counts when it has every candle present and at least 80% of the minutes across the row. Row-days just after a contract change are left out, because their averages would mix two contracts.

    Nine measurements are read on the row's own candles: how one-way it was (close minus open, as a share of the high–low range); its size against a usual row of the 20 earlier trade dates (10 or 60 by a button); closes on the wrong side of the 20MA and of the 5MA; crossings of the 20MA that came back without reaching a band ("failed crossings") and those that reached one; how many bands were touched; how much consecutive candles overlap.

    The rule. First match wins; every row of every day gets exactly one label. Defaults:

    OrderLabelWhenDefault
    1Whipsaw (dead)The row is too small against a usual rowunder half
    2TrendIt ends far from its open, and it held its averagesends at least 60% of its range from its open; at most 1 close on the wrong side of the 20MA; no close on the wrong side of the 5MA
    3Whipsaw (broken trend)One-way, but it broke an averageyour rule: "if it breaks 20MA … make it choppy". The broken-trend switch sends these to rows 4 and 5 instead.
    4Whipsaw (by likelihood)Whipsaw likelihood at or above the cutcut 50
    5SwingEverything else

    Wrong-side closes in the first third of a row (two candles of six) are forgiven while the move has not started; after that every one counts. A crossing is counted in the row where it ends.

    The whipsaw likelihood is an index from 0 to 100 for rows that are neither dead nor one-way: the weighted mean of four signs (failed crossings 50, no band reached 15, overlapping candles 20, small row 15). At or above your cut the row is a whipsaw, below it a swing. It is built by hand; it is not a probability.

    The fixed whipsaw share replaces the cut when you choose it: 60 or 70 in 100 are whipsaw. Every row of every day in your hours is ranked: clean trends first (the more one-way and the bigger, the higher), then everything else that is not dead (the bigger and the less choppy, the higher). The best 40 or 30 in 100 are kept; the rest count as whipsaw. It is a selection made looking back over all ten years: every day is ranked against all the others at once, later years included.

    The score. +3, +1 or −1 for each day, averaged per row and shown per 100 days. Moving the cut, a weight or a threshold relabels the ten years at once; thresholds are kept per chart and scoring timeframe.

    One row, worked through

    A half-hour row on 5-minute candles (six candles), with a US data release in it. Is it under half a usual row? No, so it is not dead. Does it end at least 60% of its range from its open? Yes, so it is one-way. After the two forgiven candles, does a close fall on the wrong side of the 5MA? One does, so it broke an average: by your rule a whipsaw (broken trend). With no such close it would be a trend. With the broken-trend switch on, it goes to the likelihood instead: at or above the cut (50) a whipsaw, below it a swing.

    The levels are not comparable across the columns: the rows hold different numbers of candles, and the 20MA spans a different stretch of time on each chart. Zero is not a baseline: almost every row scores above zero because +3 and +1 outweigh −1. Compare the order of the hours, not the scores.

    The order of the hours, at the defaults

    • Similar in both halves of the ten years at the defaults. 2015–2021 against 2022–2026 on 5-minute candles in half-hour rows, rank correlation inside 12:00 to 01:00 Singapore: 0.78 in the US winter and 0.66 in the US summer; over the whole day 0.82 and 0.81. A rank correlation of 1 means the same order, 0 unrelated orders. This is a stability check, not a test: the defaults were chosen with both halves in view.
    • Noise. Each half hour has 840 to 1,575 days per season. The noise of one score is about 5 points per 100 days in the US winter and 3.5 in the US summer. These figures do not allow for neighbouring days being alike: quiet and busy days come in runs, so the true noise is larger.
    • At your own settings these figures do not apply. The card's answer "when to watch" carries its own noise and its own check on both halves, at the settings in force.

    Only the best 40 or 30 in 100

    With the whipsaw share fixed at 60 in 100 on the 5-minute chart, the kept half hours of your day are, in the US summer, mostly 20:00 to 22:30 SGT (kept on 58 to 69 days in 100; 08:00 to 10:30 New York) and least often 12:00 to 13:00 SGT (18 to 23 in 100). In the US winter the same New York hours come one hour later on your clock: 21:00 to 23:00 SGT are kept on 58 to 71 days in 100. At 70 in 100 the same hours lead with lower counts (43 to 57 at the top, about 16 at the bottom). The ranking rewards size, so it leans towards the hours when gold moves most. It is a selection made looking back over all ten years.

    Charts compared and the fixed-rule trades
    • The same half hour, two charts. Of 100 half hours, the 5-minute and the 1-minute chart gave the same label on 64. With the default broken-trend rule they never disagree between trend and swing (both use the same open, close, high and low of the half hour); with the broken-trend switch on, this was not measured. They disagree on which one-way half hours broke an average, and on swing against whipsaw.
    • The order survives the chart, at the defaults. The 5-minute and the 1-minute chart rank the half hours alike: inside your hours 0.81 (US winter) and 0.92 (US summer); over the whole day 0.84 and 0.92.
    • The lookback hardly matters. Measuring "a usual row" over 10, 20 or 60 earlier days leaves the order of the hours the same (rank correlation 0.99 to 1.00).
    • What came after a reading. Measured the same way for every chart, in your hours: after a trend reading the next half hour had a clean one-way move of at least usual size 22 times in 100; after a swing reading 22; after a whipsaw reading 20; after any half hour 21. The next half hour was dead (under half the usual size) 3, 4 and 8 times in 100, against 5 after any half hour. The 1-, 5- and 15-minute charts give nearly the same figures. A reading describes the half hour that is over; it says little about the next one, except that a whipsaw is somewhat more often followed by a dead half hour.

    Your two trades as fixed rules

    Your two trade types were run as mechanical rules on each chart, with no judgement and no tuned number. Band fade: an order rests at the Bollinger band of the last finished candle; stop one standard deviation past it; target the 20MA. Pullback: after ten closes in a row on one side of the 20MA, an order rests at the 20MA; stop one standard deviation past it; target the band. Both risk 1 to make 2. An order is filled only when price trades a tick through it; a stop and a target in the same minute count as a loss; a stop costs one tick of slippage; one trade at a time; at most 24 candles; entries only in your hours and flat by 01:00 SGT.

    Dollars per ounce; entries in your hours, ten years. "Usual risk" is the middle case of the distance from entry to stop.

    • What it shows. They lost on every chart. With a stop one standard deviation away, about a quarter of the trades reached a target twice as far; a third would be needed to break even before costs. Every filled trade starts a tick offside and a stop costs a tick of slippage, so the slower the chart, the wider the stop and the less those ticks and the costs weigh: the loss after costs is about two thirds of the risk on the 1-minute fade, a third on the 5-minute, under a quarter on the 15-minute.
    • What the reading before the entry added. Little. On the 5-minute fade 24 to 26 trades in 100 won whether the half hour before was a trend, a swing or a whipsaw.
    • What it cannot show. How you trade. You choose which touches to take; these rules take every one. Nothing here is advice.
    Limits

    What the labels are

    • After the fact. A label needs the whole row. At 21:30 you cannot know which label today's row will get; the score only says how often each kind has happened at that time.
    • Short rows are coarse. On rows of four or six candles one failed crossing fills that sign of the likelihood; at the default weight (50) and cut (50) that alone makes the row a whipsaw. A single news candle that makes most of a row's range can earn a trend in hindsight.
    • The 20MA of the 5-minute chart is slow. It spans 100 minutes. A clean one-way half hour that starts on the far side of it counts as a broken trend, so by your rule a whipsaw: 2.7 row-days in 100. Judged by the scale instead (the switch), 82 in 100 of those would be swings.
    • Hard clock boundaries. A move that straddles two rows is split between them.
    • Hand-set thresholds. The 60%, the "under half", the ramps and the weights were chosen by eye. Your own fitted settings come from examples on the 1-minute chart: carried over unchanged to the 5-minute chart they would label 74 half hours in 100 whipsaw. Whether "whipsaw" here means what you mean is tested only by the examples you label in "Teach it your eye".
    • Swing is what is left over. It means "not dead, not one-way, not choppy enough". Nothing requires price to travel band to band.

    What the score is not

    • Not profit and loss. +3 / +1 / −1 are your points, not dollars. The page shows scores and counts and leaves it to you to judge whether an hour can be traded at a profit.
    • Mostly a volatility clock. The top half hours are the busy ones (the London, US data and New York open times), and the fixed-share ranking, which rewards size, leans to the same hours. A few rank by structure rather than size, for example 13:30 SGT. How much the score tells beside how much gold moves has not been measured.
    • Not comparable across charts or scoring timeframes.

    Statistics

    • One sample. The rules, the defaults and the charts were chosen while looking at the same ten years they are scored on. The two halves are a stability check, not a test; only new days can test them. The held-back recent file has 115 trade dates, 27 April to 13 November 2026, with no data from 27 May to 24 June 2026; it plays no part in the score.
    • Days are not independent. Quiet and busy days come in runs, so the true noise is larger than the figures shown.
    • Many settings. With three charts, a cut, four weights, five thresholds, three lookbacks and a fixed share, some setting will always make a favourite hour look best. Changing settings to fit a hunch is not evidence.
    • The fixed share looks back. It is a selection made looking back over all ten years: each day is ranked with later years in the pool.

    Data

    • Size is measured against the whole day. Early-afternoon Singapore rows are "dead" far more often, which may be exactly what you mean by untradable, or may hide a good quiet-hours range.
    • Release days are not separated in the score. The top half hours sit on the US data-release and open times. The fixed-rule trades are split into news days and other days on the page.
    • One file, one contract per day. Prices are unadjusted; row-days just after a contract change are left out. A crossing can still carry a move from before a contract change into a later row; how many rows that touches has not been counted.
    • Coverage. A row counts when it has every candle present and at least 80% of the minutes across the row, so one candle can be thin. Thin rows are left out; whether that raises or lowers a row's score has not been shown.

    The fixed-rule trades

    • Assumed fills. Real fills at a band can be better or worse than "a tick through, at the limit". Stops and targets inside one minute are resolved against the trade.
    • Tiny stops. On the 1-minute chart the stop is about five ticks. 8,902 fade trades there had a stop of one tick and lost on the entry minute by construction.
    • Many tables. The study printed 6,840 table cells. Among so many, some half hour will look good for no reason; none was picked out.
    How it was checked
    • 17 November 2026, the method. A second, plain implementation of the nine measurements, written from the written rules, was run on 240 real trade dates (30 June 2020 to 9 July 2021): 11,040 row-days on the 5-minute chart and 5,520 on the 15-minute chart, every stored value equal. The stored 1-minute sets equal the previous build apart from the added lookbacks. The fixed-rule trades have 76 hand-worked cases. The unit tests were written from the written rules, not from the code.
    • 17 November 2026, outside critique. The design was given to an outside reviewer to attack. Adopted: a row is judged on its own candles (the first design added three candles either side); one-hour rows for the 15-minute chart; the ranking for the fixed share; strict fills, one trade at a time and a capped hold for the fixed-rule trades; counts of days on every figure. Declined: relaxing your rule that a break of the 20MA ends a trend (the case is counted instead, under Limits).
    • Each test run. The tables and the after-a-reading figures in this note are checked against the stored results.
    • 21 November 2026, this version. Three reviews of the method were read and this note was cut to one screen and folds. Corrected: the order of the hours is said as measured at the defaults, the figures inside your hours first; the noise figures are named as not allowing for neighbouring days being alike; "never trend against swing" holds for the default broken-trend rule only; the coverage rule is said exactly; the fixed share is named a selection made looking back; the held-back file is described from its own record.
